## Convergence in Norm

Recall that a [[normed-space|norm]] is a function $\Vert \cdot\Vert$ from a
vector (function) space $V$ to $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying, for all $f,g\in V$ and
$a \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. $\Vert f\Vert \geq 0$, and $\Vert f\Vert=0$ if and only if $f=0$;
2. $\Vert af\Vert = |a|\Vert f\Vert$;
3. $\Vert f+g \Vert \leq\Vert f\Vert +\Vert g\Vert$ (triangle inequality).

:::{.definition data-title="Convergence in Norm"}

A sequence $\{f_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ in a normed space $(V, \Vert\cdot\Vert)$
**converges in norm** to $f$, written $f_n\stackrel{\Vert\cdot\Vert}{\to}f$, if
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Vert f_n-f\Vert=0.
$$

:::

## Convergence in $L^p$ Norm (r-th Mean)

The $L^p$ norm is the norm linked to probability spaces and expectations, see
[[lp-spaces]] and [[lp-norm]]. For a random variable $X$ on
$(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ and $p\geq1$,
$$
\Vert X\Vert_{p}=[\mathbb{E}|X|^p]^{1/p}=\left(\int _{\Omega}|X|^p \, d\mathbb{P}\right)^{1/p} .
$$

:::{.definition data-title="Convergence in $L^p$ Norm"}

A sequence of random variables $\{ X_{n} \}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ with
$\mathbb{E}|X_n|^p<\infty$ **converges in $L^p$ norm**, or **in $p$-th mean**,
to $X$, written $X_{n}\stackrel{L^p}{\to}X$, if
$$
\lim_{ n \to \infty }\Vert X_{n}-X\Vert_{p}=0,\quad\text{equivalently}\quad\lim_{ n \to \infty } \mathbb{E}|X_{n}-X|^p = 0.
$$

:::

Convergence in $p$-th mean is convergence of integrals (expectations) and is
exactly convergence in norm on $L^p$. Random variables can also converge
[[convergence-almost-surely|almost surely]],
[[convergence-in-probability|in probability]] and
[[convergence-in-law|in law]]; the relationships between all modes are in
[[convergence-of-random-variables]].

## Relationships

:::{.theorem data-title="$L^s\implies L^r$ for $1\leq r<s<\infty$"}

If $X_{n}\stackrel{L^s}{\to}X$ and $1\leq r<s<\infty$ then
$X_{n}\stackrel{L^r}{\to}X$. In other words, higher orders of convergence
imply lower orders.

:::

:::{.proof}

By [[lyapunov-inequality]] applied to $|X_n-X|$,
$$
(\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^r)^{1/r}\leq(\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^s)^{1/s}\to0.
$$
Alternatively, apply [[jensen-inequality]] with the convex function
$f(x)=x^{s/r}$ to $|X_n-X|^r$.

:::

The converse does not hold in general.

:::{.theorem data-title="$L^1\implies$ convergence in probability"}

If $X_{n}\stackrel{L^1}{\to}X$ then $X_{n}\stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\to}X$.

:::

:::{.proof}

By the [[markov-inequality]], for every $\epsilon>0$
$$
\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}-X|>\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\epsilon}\cdot \mathbb{E}|X_{n}-X|\to0.
$$

:::

:::{.example data-title="Converse fails"}

On $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure let $X_n=n\mathbb{1}_{(0,1/n)}$. Then
$X_n\to0$ almost surely and in probability, but $\mathbb{E}|X_n|=1$ for all
$n$, so $X_n\not\to0$ in $L^1$.

:::

The converse holds under [[uniform-integrability]].

:::{.theorem data-title="Convergence in $\mathbb{P}$ and in $L^p$ under uniform integrability"}

For $p>0$ assume that $X_n \in L^p$, $n \geq 1$ and
$X_{n}\stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\to} X$. The following are equivalent:

1. $\{ |X_{n}|^p,~n\geq 1 \}$ is uniformly integrable;
2. $X_{n}\stackrel{L^p}{\to}X$ and $X\in L^p$; and
3. $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[|X_{n}|^p]=\mathbb{E}[|X|^p]<\infty$.

:::
